fetched_contents.text: Larkspur Poisoning of Cattle: Plant and Animal Factors that Influence Plant Toxicity Introduction Toxic larkspurs (Delphinium species) poison and kill cattle in western North America, and cattle deaths from larkspur poisoning can be as high as 15%.1 Millions of dollars are lost from ranching communities due to animal deaths, increased management costs, and the underutilization of nutritious rangelands. Economic costs of larkspur poisoning to ranchers is not only associated with cow deaths, but, for example, other costs include loss of that cow nursing a healthy calf. The rancher must keep the calf alive, and if it survives there is lost income from marketing an early weaned, poor-performing calf. Ranchers must also replace the dead cow to keep herd numbers constant. Ranchers managing cattle on rangelands with large populations of toxic larkspur are seeking solutions to the larkspur problem. The Poisonous Plant Research Laboratory (PPRL) in Logan, Utah is investigating how to reduce larkspur poisoning of cattle. We provide a brief review of basic information about larkspur and larkspur poisoning of cattle and describe recent research advances and solutions for larkspur poisoning of cattle. Current management recommendations1 for grazing cattle on ranges containing larkspur are based on the concentration of toxic alkaloids in the larkspur, the quantity of larkspur eaten, and the rate at which larkspur is eaten by cattle. Until recently, we have not considered animal factors, including breed, age, and sex, which research has shown may play a role in cattle poisoning. The Plants Larkspurs belong to the buttercup plant family and are identified by their characteristic flower that has a spur, hence the name larkspur (Fig. 1). There are 60 native species of larkspurs in North America that have been divided into three groups: tall, low, and plains.2 Most cattle deaths are caused by tall larkspur (Fig. 2A and 2B) but low larkspur (Fig. 2C) can poison cattle during cool, wet, springs when growth conditions are optimal for these species (Table 1).3 Table 1. These plants grow in mountain rangelands and begin flowering from mid to late July when they have reached 80% of their maximum height. Their flowering ends three weeks later when they enter the pod stage. Tall larkspurs produce large numbers of seedpods and seeds with high concentrations of toxins.1 Low larkspur Low larkspurs are 20 to 60 cm in height and have small, fine, leaves (Table 1). These plants grow in desert shrub, mountain brush, sagebrush, and pinion-juniper communities during the spring and early summer. Low larkspur populations increase when late winters and springs are cool and wet.4 This is a problem, because, during cool wet weather, the growth of grasses is delayed resulting in fewer alternative forages leading to increased consumption and deaths of grazing cattle. Plains larkspur Plains larkspur are about 80 cm tall and have small, fine leaves like low larkspur (Table 1). This larkspur grows on foothills and short grass prairie ranges in Wyoming, Colorado, and northern New Mexico.5 Plains larkspur starts to grow early in the spring, and then matures later into summer when cattle often consume fatal quantities.5 Toxins Present in Larkspurs Larkspurs contain toxic compounds termed alkaloids (i.e., nitrogen containing hydrocarbons) that are produced by and accumulated in the plant. These toxins are in the stems, leaves, flowers, and seedpods, all of which are eaten by cattle.1 Two principle classes of alkaloids in larkspur are the toxic N-(methylsuccinimido) anthranoyllycoctonine type (MSAL-type) and the less toxic non-MSAL type.1 The dominant MSAL-type alkaloid is called methyllycaconitine (MLA). In general, MSAL-type alkaloids like MLA, must be present in larkspur plants to poison cattle. Welch et al.6, 7 have shown that the non-MSAL-type alkaloids can increase the toxicity of MSAL-type alkaloids in cattle. Welch et al.6, 7 have also shown that the chemical profiles and alkaloid concentration vary from location to location. Though alkaloid mixtures have different toxicities, the plants with higher MSAL-alkaloid concentrations have a higher potential risk to poison cattle.4 Clinical Signs of Larkspur Poisoning in Cattle The clinical signs of larkspur poisoning in cattle are caused by plant toxins blocking nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChR) to prevent the neurotransmitter acetylcholine from activating nerve and muscle cells.8 As the larkspur toxins begin to react with muscles and nerves, cattle show clinical signs of poisoning. Authors Affiliation * 1 Poisonous Plant Research Laboratory, ARS, USDA, Logan, UT 84341, USA. jpfister@cc.usu.edu * PMID: 10091130 Abstract Larkspurs (Delphinium spp.) are toxic plants that contain numerous diterpenoid alkaloids which occur as one of two structural types: (1) lycotonine, and (2) 7,8-methylenedioxylycoctonine (MDL-type). Among the lycoctonine type alkaloids are three N-(methylsuccinimido) anthranoyllycoctonine (MSAL-type) alkaloids which appear to be most toxic: methyllycaconitine (MLA), 14-deacetylnudicauline (DAN), and nudicauline. An ester function at C-18 is an important structural requirement for toxicity. Intoxication results from neuromuscular paralysis, as nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in the muscle and brain are blocked by toxic alkaloids. Clinical signs include labored breathing, rapid and irregular heartbeat, muscular weakness, and collapse. Toxic alkaloid concentration generally declines in tall larkspurs with maturation, but alkaloid concentration varies over years and from plant to plant, and is of little use for predicting consumption by cattle. Knowledge of toxic alkaloid concentration is valuable for management purposes when cattle begin to eat larkspur. Cattle generally begin consuming tall larkspur after flowering racemes are elongated, and consumption increases as larkspur matures. Weather is also a major factor in cattle consumption, as cattle tend to eat more larkspur during or just after summer storms. Management options that may be useful for livestock producers include conditioning cattle to avoid larkspur (food aversion learning), grazing tall larkspur ranges before flowering (early grazing) and after seed shatter (late grazing), grazing sheep before cattle, herbicidal control of larkspur plants, and drug therapy for intoxicated animals. Some potentially fruitful research avenues include examining alkaloid chemistry in low and plains larkspurs, developing immunologic methods for analyzing larkspur alkaloids, developing drug therapy, and devising grazing regimes specifically for low and plains larkspur. fetched_contents.text: Retrospective study of cattle poisonings in California: recognition, diagnosis, and treatment Abstract In this retrospective study all suspect bovine intoxications submitted to the California Animal Health and Food Safety Laboratory between January 1, 2000 and December 31, 2011 were reviewed. A total of 1199 cases were submitted, but a diagnosis of intoxication was only established in 13.5% of cases. In these cases, overexposures to minerals, metals, and poisonous plants were determined as the most commonly diagnosed poisonings in cattle in California. Nitrate/nitrite poisoning was the most commonly diagnosed plant-associated intoxication, followed by gossypol and oleander. This study details the diagnostic challenges and treatment options for the most commonly diagnosed intoxications. To ensure proper treatment and prevention of new cases, accurate diagnosis is necessary, and therefore this review provides an essential tool for the food animal practitioner. Available toxicological analyses are offered at select laboratories, which can be time consuming and expensive, yet the potential for residues in consumed animal products and implications for human health necessitate testing and consultation. Any potential exposure to a toxicant in cattle should be reviewed to determine whether a residue hazard exists. Therapy focuses on immediate removal of the toxicant from the environment and from the gastrointestinal tract. With few antidotes available, most are cost prohibitive to treat numerous affected cattle. In addition, most antidotes will require extra-label drug use and establishment of meat and milk withdrawal times. Keywords: toxins, toxicology, poisonous plants, bovine Introduction Although infrequent in practice, food animal intoxications require extensive diagnostic and rapid therapeutic measures. The diagnostic approach is key for adequate treatment and prevention of further cases. Unfortunately, no single procedure will test for all toxicants, and these cases require a multifaceted approach to assemble and solve a diagnostic puzzle. A complete case history, clinical and clinicopathological data, postmortem findings, chemical analyses, and occasionally bioassay findings all provide pieces of this puzzle.1 Toxic residues in food animals may pose a public health risk in edible products. In addition and have to diagnosis and treatment, practitioners often face publicity and medico-legal issues consult closely with regulatory agencies on food safety and public health. Crucial in complex cases, referral veterinary toxicology laboratories can help the bovine practitioner establish an accurate diagnosis and provide advice regarding food safety. In this report, we review and organize existing data from cattle poisonings in California, identify the most common toxicants, and aim to provide a tool for bovine practitioners to enable early recognition, rapid diagnosis and confident treatment. The purpose of this study was to characterize the most commonly diagnosed intoxications of cattle in California, and to provide details on diagnostic work-up and treatment in view of public health risks. ## What tall larkspur and similar plants are, and how they harm cattle

Tall larkspur is a major toxic plant of concern for cattle, and it belongs to the buttercup family. The evidence identifies tall larkspur as one of several larkspur species that poison cattle, with tall larkspurs typically being 70 to 200 cm in height and having large hollow stems and wide-bladed leaves [N1-F1]. The article also notes that larkspurs are divided into three groups: tall, low, and plains, and that most cattle deaths are caused by tall larkspur while low larkspur and plains larkspur can also poison cattle under favorable conditions [N1-F1]. Related species include Sierra larkspur, Subalpine larkspur, Smooth larkspur, and others, each with different heights, elevations, plant communities, and risk levels [N1-F1].

### Which plant species are typically involved and why they are palatable

The main species involved in cattle poisoning are tall larkspurs, with low larkspurs and plains larkspurs also contributing under certain environmental conditions [N1-F1]. The evidence explains that larkspur toxicity is highest at the vegetative/bud stage and decreases as the plant matures, but palatability increases during this period [N6-R3]. This combination of high toxicity and increased palatability makes larkspur especially dangerous. The same source also notes that larkspur populations can increase when late winters and springs are cool and wet, which delays grass growth and increases cattle consumption [N1-F1]. Another source states that some poisonous plants are highly palatable to livestock, and cattle choose plants accordingly [N3-R4]. Taken together, these sources show that cattle are at risk because larkspur is both chemically toxic and palatable, especially during early growth stages.

### What neurotoxic compounds they contain and their mode of action

Larkspurs contain toxic compounds termed alkaloids, specifically norditerpenoid alkaloids [N1-R3]. The evidence identifies two principle classes of alkaloids: MSAL-type and non-MSAL-type, with the dominant MSAL-type alkaloid being methyllycaconitine (MLA) [N1-F1]. It also notes that Welch et al. have shown that non-MSAL-type alkaloids can increase the toxicity of MSAL-type alkaloids in cattle [N1-R5]. The mode of action is neuromuscular blockade at nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, preventing acetylcholine from activating nerve and muscle cells [N2-F2]. The PubMed article states that this results in neuromuscular paralysis, with clinical signs caused by plant toxins blocking nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in the muscle and brain [N2-F2]. A direct search result adds that the alkaloids act principally at the neuromuscular junction, causing a curare-like blockade with resulting muscle weakness and paralysis [N2-R2]. These mechanisms explain why larkspur poisoning causes muscle weakness, coordination loss, and paralysis.

### How toxic exposure is acquired and why cattle are at risk

Exposure occurs through ingestion of larkspur plant material, including stems, leaves, flowers, and seedpods [N1-F1]. The evidence emphasizes that cattle begin consuming tall larkspur after flowering racemes are elongated, and consumption increases as the plant matures [N2-F2]. Weather also plays a major role, as cattle tend to eat more larkspur during or just after summer storms [N2-F2]. This means cattle are at risk not only because larkspur is palatable but also because grazing conditions can drive selective feeding on larkspur when alternative forage is scarce or delayed [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that cattle grazing behavior and plant preference matter, with the preference for green plant material being extremely strong and animals grazing less preferred material when choice is reduced [N3-R1][N3-R2]. In other words, cattle are at risk because larkspur is both attractive and toxic, and because grazing behavior can push them to consume more of it under unfavorable conditions [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R4].

## Bottom line
Tall larkspur and related species are among the main neurotoxic plants that harm cattle. They are harmful because they contain potent alkaloids that block nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, causing paralysis and death. Cattle are at risk because larkspur is palatable, especially during early growth stages, and because grazing behavior, weather, and forage availability can increase consumption [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R4].

## Management practices to prevent or reduce poisoning

### Effective grazing management strategies

The evidence supports a grazing management approach focused on reducing exposure before cattle consume larkspur. One source states that management options include conditioning cattle to avoid larkspur through food aversion learning, grazing tall larkspur ranges before flowering, and grazing after seed shatter [N2-F2]. Another source recommends conditioning cattle to avoid larkspur [N2-F2]. The grazing approach is also tied to weather and plant maturity: cattle eat more larkspur during or just after summer storms, so managing grazing timing can reduce exposure [N2-F2]. The evidence also highlights the importance of good pasture management to keep losses at a minimum [N2-R4]. Additional grazing management guidance emphasizes controlled grazing systems to improve pasture health, maximize forage utilization, and increase livestock productivity [N5-R1]. Rotational grazing is also presented as a useful tool for integrating fencing systems with livestock handling facilities and improving pasture health [N5-R3][N5-R5].

### Diagnostic and treatment options available

The California retrospective study on cattle poisonings emphasizes that specialized veterinary toxicology laboratories may provide testing for plant toxins, but the assays do not cover the wide variety of plant toxins [N4-R1]. The same study notes that diagnostic challenges are common, and accurate diagnosis is essential for treatment and prevention [N4-F3]. It also states that referral veterinary toxicology laboratories can help establish an accurate diagnosis and provide advice on food safety [N4-F3]. In practical terms, the evidence suggests that diagnosis often relies on a multifaceted approach, including a complete case history, clinical and clinicopathological data, postmortem findings, toxicological results, and occasionally bioassay findings [N4-F3]. However, the evidence also indicates that laboratory testing is time-consuming and expensive, and that most antidotes are cost prohibitive, require extra-label drug use, and need meat and milk withdrawal times [N4-F3].

### What to do if poisoning is suspected

If poisoning is suspected, the evidence points to immediate action: remove the toxicant from the environment and from the gastrointestinal tract [N4-F3]. It also recommends careful case review to determine whether a residue hazard exists, and consultation with regulatory agencies on food safety and public health [N4-F3]. The evidence also notes that diagnosis and treatment often involve referral to veterinary toxicology laboratories, which can help establish an accurate diagnosis and provide treatment guidance [N4-F3]. The larkspur-specific context adds that sudden deaths of cattle on summer range at higher altitudes where larkspur is abundant should prompt suspicion of larkspur poisoning [N6-R5].

## Bottom line
Prevention and management depend on timing, grazing strategy, and early detection. Best practices include grazing before flowering, after seed shatter, and using food aversion learning; conditioning cattle to avoid larkspur; and managing pastures with controlled or rotational grazing [N2-F2][N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-R5]. Diagnosis requires specialized toxicology testing and a multifaceted approach, while treatment emphasizes removal of the toxicant and consultation with veterinary toxicology services [N4-R1][N4-F3]. If poisoning is suspected, prompt diagnosis and public health consultation are essential [N4-F3][N6-R5].

## Clinical patterns and consequences in affected cattle

### Typical signs and symptoms seen in poisoned cattle

The evidence is consistent on the clinical picture of larkspur poisoning. Typical signs include trembling, lack of coordination, rapid heart rate, and collapse [N1-F1]. The PubMed article states that clinical signs are caused by plant toxins blocking nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, resulting in neuromuscular paralysis [N2-F2]. Another source notes that clinical signs include labored breathing, rapid and irregular heartbeat, muscular weakness, and collapse [N2-F1]. The same PubMed article adds that in single-dose exposures, signs occur 7 to 24 hours after eating [N1-F1]. A general livestock poisoning source also reports muscular weakness, collapse, and difficulty breathing as symptoms [N2-R1]. These signs are consistent with curare-like neuromuscular blockade and severe paralysis.

### How illness progresses over time

The evidence describes a progression from early signs to severe collapse. In single-dose exposures, signs appear within 7 to 24 hours after ingestion [N1-F1]. The PubMed article also notes that clinical signs are caused by plant toxins beginning to react with muscles and nerves [N1-F1]. The progression is thus rapid and cumulative: initial tremors and coordination loss progress to muscle weakness, inability to stand, and then collapse [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The evidence does not provide a full timeline beyond this, but it clearly shows that poisoning develops quickly after ingestion and leads to severe neuromuscular failure.

### Which animals are most at risk and why

The evidence suggests that cattle are most at risk when larkspur is highly palatable and when alternative forage is limited. The larkspur poisoning review explains that larkspur is highly palatable to cattle, especially during the flower stage, and that heavy losses occur when it is highly palatable and in infested grazing areas [N1-R4]. The same review notes that cattle begin consuming tall larkspur after flowering racemes are elongated, and consumption increases as the plant matures [N2-F2]. It also states that cattle tend to eat more larkspur during or just after summer storms [N2-F2]. This pattern means young or lactating cattle may be especially vulnerable when forage is scarce, as they are more likely to select larkspur under pressure.

The evidence also points to management factors as important. The California poisoning study notes that cattle generally begin consuming tall larkspur after flowering racemes are elongated and that consumption increases with maturity [N2-F2]. The evidence also indicates that cattle grazing behavior, especially when green material is present, can strongly influence feeding choices [N3-R1][N3-R4]. In other words, cattle at risk are those exposed to larkspur during periods when it is palatable and when forage is limited, and those with grazing behaviors that increase selective feeding on larkspur [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R4].

## Bottom line
Affected cattle typically show trembling, lack of coordination, rapid heart rate, muscular weakness, and collapse, with signs appearing within 7 to 24 hours after ingestion [N1-F1][N2-F1][N2-F2]. Illness progresses quickly from early neuromuscular signs to collapse. Animals most at risk are those exposed when larkspur is highly palatable, forage is limited, and cattle selectively consume larkspur under grazing pressure [N1-R4][N2-F2][N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R4].

## What tall larkspur and similar plants are, and how they harm cattle

Tall larkspur is a major toxic plant of concern for cattle, and it belongs to the buttercup family. The evidence identifies tall larkspur as one of several larkspur species that poison cattle, with tall larkspurs typically being 70 to 200 cm in height and having large hollow stems and wide-bladed leaves [N1-F1]. The article also notes that larkspurs are divided into three groups: tall, low, and plains, and that most cattle deaths are caused by tall larkspur while low larkspur and plains larkspur can also poison cattle under favorable conditions [N1-F1]. Related species include Sierra larkspur, Subalpine larkspur, Smooth larkspur, and others, each with different heights, elevations, plant communities, and risk levels [N1-F1].

### Which plant species are typically involved and why they are palatable

The main species involved in cattle poisoning are tall larkspurs, with low larkspurs and plains larkspurs also contributing under certain environmental conditions [N1-F1]. The evidence explains that larkspur toxicity is highest at the vegetative/bud stage and decreases as the plant matures, but palatability increases during this period [N6-R3]. This combination of high toxicity and increased palatability makes larkspur especially dangerous. The same source also notes that larkspur populations can increase when late winters and springs are cool and wet, which delays grass growth and increases cattle consumption [N1-F1]. Another source states that some poisonous plants are highly palatable to livestock, and cattle choose plants accordingly [N3-R4]. Taken together, these sources show that cattle are at risk because larkspur is both chemically toxic and palatable, especially during early growth stages.

### What neurotoxic compounds they contain and their mode of action

Larkspurs contain toxic compounds termed alkaloids, specifically norditerpenoid alkaloids [N1-R3]. The evidence identifies two principle classes of alkaloids: MSAL-type and non-MSAL-type, with the dominant MSAL-type alkaloid being methyllycaconitine (MLA) [N1-F1]. It also notes that Welch et al. have shown that non-MSAL-type alkaloids can increase the toxicity of MSAL-type alkaloids in cattle [N1-R5]. The mode of action is neuromuscular blockade at nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, preventing acetylcholine from activating nerve and muscle cells [N2-F2]. The PubMed article states that this results in neuromuscular paralysis, with clinical signs caused by plant toxins blocking nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in the muscle and brain [N2-F2]. A direct search result adds that the alkaloids act principally at the neuromuscular junction, causing a curare-like blockade with resulting muscle weakness and paralysis [N2-R2]. These mechanisms explain why larkspur poisoning causes muscle weakness, coordination loss, and paralysis.

### How toxic exposure is acquired and why cattle are at risk

Exposure occurs through ingestion of larkspur plant material, including stems, leaves, flowers, and seedpods [N1-F1]. The evidence emphasizes that cattle begin consuming tall larkspur after flowering racemes are elongated, and consumption increases as the plant matures [N2-F2]. Weather also plays a major role, as cattle tend to eat more larkspur during or just after summer storms [N2-F2]. This means cattle are at risk not only because larkspur is palatable but also because grazing conditions can drive selective feeding on larkspur when alternative forage is scarce or delayed [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that cattle grazing behavior and plant preference matter, with the preference for green plant material being extremely strong and animals grazing less preferred material when choice is reduced [N3-R1][N3-R2]. In other words, cattle are at risk because larkspur is both attractive and toxic, and because grazing behavior can push them to consume more of it under unfavorable conditions [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R4].

## Bottom line
Tall larkspur and related species are among the main neurotoxic plants that harm cattle. They are harmful because they contain potent alkaloids that block nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, causing paralysis and death. Cattle are at risk because larkspur is palatable, especially during early growth stages, and because grazing behavior, weather, and forage availability can increase consumption [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R4].

## Management practices to prevent or reduce poisoning

### Effective grazing management strategies

The evidence supports a grazing management approach focused on reducing exposure before cattle consume larkspur. One source states that management options include conditioning cattle to avoid larkspur through food aversion learning, grazing tall larkspur ranges before flowering, and grazing after seed shatter [N2-F2]. Another source recommends conditioning cattle to avoid larkspur [N2-F2]. The grazing approach is also tied to weather and plant maturity: cattle eat more larkspur during or just after summer storms, so managing grazing timing can reduce exposure [N2-F2]. The evidence also highlights the importance of good pasture management to keep losses at a minimum [N2-R4]. Additional grazing management guidance emphasizes controlled grazing systems to improve pasture health, maximize forage utilization, and increase livestock productivity [N5-R1]. Rotational grazing is also presented as a useful tool for integrating fencing systems with livestock handling facilities and improving pasture health [N5-R3][N5-R5].

### Diagnostic and treatment options available

The California retrospective study on cattle poisonings emphasizes that specialized veterinary toxicology laboratories may provide testing for plant toxins, but the assays do not cover the wide variety of plant toxins [N4-R1]. The same study notes that diagnostic challenges are common, and accurate diagnosis is essential for treatment and prevention [N4-F3]. It also states that referral veterinary toxicology laboratories can help establish an accurate diagnosis and provide advice on food safety [N4-F3]. In practical terms, the evidence suggests that diagnosis often relies on a multifaceted approach, including a complete case history, clinical and clinicopathological data, postmortem findings, toxicological results, and occasionally bioassay findings [N4-F3]. However, the evidence also indicates that laboratory testing is time-consuming and expensive, and that most antidotes are cost prohibitive, require extra-label drug use, and need meat and milk withdrawal times [N4-F3].

### What to do if poisoning is suspected

If poisoning is suspected, the evidence points to immediate action: remove the toxicant from the environment and from the gastrointestinal tract [N4-F3]. It also recommends careful case review to determine whether a residue hazard exists, and consultation with regulatory agencies on food safety and public health [N4-F3]. The evidence also notes that diagnosis and treatment often involve referral to veterinary toxicology laboratories, which can help establish an accurate diagnosis and provide treatment guidance [N4-F3]. The larkspur-specific context adds that sudden deaths of cattle on summer range at higher altitudes where larkspur is abundant should prompt suspicion of larkspur poisoning [N6-R5].

## Bottom line
Prevention and management depend on timing, grazing strategy, and early detection. Best practices include grazing before flowering, after seed shatter, and using food aversion learning; conditioning cattle to avoid larkspur; and managing pastures with controlled or rotational grazing [N2-F2][N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-R5]. Diagnosis requires specialized toxicology testing and a multifaceted approach, while treatment emphasizes removal of the toxicant and consultation with veterinary toxicology services [N4-R1][N4-F3]. If poisoning is suspected, prompt diagnosis and public health consultation are essential [N4-F3][N6-R5].

Related species include Sierra larkspur, Subalpine larkspur, Smooth larkspur, and others, each with different heights, elevations, plant communities, and risk levels [N1-F1].

The main species involved in cattle poisoning are tall larkspurs, with low larkspurs and plains larkspurs also contributing under certain environmental conditions [N1-F1]. This combination of high toxicity and increased palatability makes larkspur especially dangerous. The same source also notes that larkspur populations can increase when late winters and springs are cool and wet, which delays grass growth and increases cattle consumption [N1-F1]. Another source states that some poisonous plants are highly palatable to livestock, and cattle choose plants accordingly [N3-R4]. Taken together, these sources show that cattle are at risk because larkspur is both chemically toxic and palatable, especially during early growth stages.

Larkspurs contain toxic compounds termed alkaloids, specifically norditerpenoid alkaloids [N1-R3]. The evidence identifies two principle classes of alkaloids: MSAL-type and non-MSAL-type, with the dominant MSAL-type alkaloid being methyllycaconitine (MLA) [N1-F1]. Tall larkspur and related species are among the main neurotoxic plants that harm cattle. They are harmful because they contain potent alkaloids that block nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, causing paralysis and death.
